ce:list-item.ce:para: Carbon films with parameter-controllable interface nanotexture were fabricated.
Interface nanotexture significantly enhanced the tribological performance of carbon films.
A super-low wear rate was achieved, with a value of 6.54 ± 0.70 × 10-8 mm3/N·m.
The interface nanotexture enhanced the adhesion strength between the film and substrate.
The nanotextured carbon film exhibited a smaller abrasive dust, which helped stabilize the frictional process.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The effect and mechanism of surface texture on friction have been extensively explored, such as storing the abrasive and reducing the real contact area. However, studying the impact of the interface texture remains crucial, especially as the texture size approaches the nanoscale. In the present work, the silicon substrate with different parameters nanotexture was fabricated using a metal-assisted chemical etching process, and the graphene sheets embedded carbon (GSEC) film was deposited on the nanotextured substrate via a low-energy electron irradiation process to produce the interface nanotextured carbon films. After the addition of the interface nanotexture, the tribological performance of carbon films exhibited significant enhancement, with the degree of improvement being influenced by the parameters of the interface nanotexture. A super-low wear rate was achieved, with a value of 6.54 ± 0.70 × 10−8 mm3/N m. The improved tribological performance is due to the enhancement of film-substrate adhesion strength facilitated by interface nanotexture, and its role in promoting the rapid formation of a stable transfer film on the counter-grinding ball. The carbon film with nanotexture displays a small size of the abrasive particles, which contributes to the stabilization of the friction process.

ce:section.ce:para: Carbon, a common element on Earth, is the basis of life and an important factor affecting the environment and climate change [1,2]. The complexity of its hybridization causes a variety of carbon allotropes, such as diamond, graphite, amorphous carbon [3–5], etc. Recently, the discovery of graphene further promoted the study of carbon materials. The graphene with a perfect 2D structure exhibits excellent optical, electrical, and mechanical properties and is considered a revolutionary material [6–8]. The special layered structure of graphene offers significant potential in friction reduction, achieving superlubricity at both the nanoscale and microscale [9,10]. Besides, the application of graphene under macroscale has garnered much attention. The conventional method of utilizing the graphene under macroscale was the spraying method, which leveraged its friction-reducing capabilities without fully utilizing its other properties [11,12]. Hence, to broaden the use of graphene, nanocrystalline carbon films were developed, incorporating graphene nanosheets into an amorphous carbon matrix. The nanocrystalline carbon films could realize the macroscale application of the graphene while preserving its excellent properties [13–15]. The graphene sheet-embedded carbon (GSEC) film stands out as a prime instance, with graphene nanocrystallite embedded in the matrix of amorphous carbon [16,17]. This film exhibits special electrical and magnetic properties, promoting its potential utilization in the nanogenerator [18] and manipulating friction through a magnetic field [19]. However, the GSEC film suffers from poor adhesion and large surface roughness, thereby compromising its anti-wear properties [16]. These limitations hinder the long-term viability of the GSEC film for practical applications.

To reinforce the anti-wear properties of the thin film, various technical processes have been explored, such as embedding interlayers [20,21], doping with other elements [22–25], utilizing multilayer film [26,27], and fabricating texture [28,29]. Texture, as a convenient and economical film modification method, has been applied widely. It has been known that the surface texture could decrease the real contact area between the contact pair and trap abrasive dust generated during friction [28–31]. Recently, researchers also have discovered that the texture fabricated on the substrate could release the internal stress within the thin film [32] and enhance the adhesion strength between the substrate and thin film [33–35]. However, the study about the nanotexture illustrated its anti-wear property was insufficient due to the nanotexture with a poor ability to trap abrasive dust, and the nanotexture would increase the surface roughness [36]. In addition, fabricating nanotextures over large areas is challenging, and the production costs are substantial. Moreover, studies about the interface nanotexture and nanotexture combined with the carbon film are rare.

In this study, the metal-assisted chemical etching process was adopted to fabricate nanotexture on the silicon substrate with controllable parameters. Subsequently, the GSEC film was deposited on nanotextured silicon using an electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) electron sputtering system to fabricate an interface nanotextured GSEC film. The surface morphologies of nanotexture on the silicon substrate and the GSEC film were characterized. The tribological performance of interface nanotextured GSEC film at room temperature was measured to reveal the impact of the nanotexture. The adhesion strength between the silicon substrate and film, and the evolution of transfer films on the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball surface were characterized to investigate the mechanism of interface nanotexture on the tribological performance of nanotextured GSEC films. A comparison of the frictional behavior among carbon films with no texture, microtexture, and nanotexture was conducted to gain a better understanding of the advantages of nanotexture.

The schematic of the fabrication process for the interface nanotextured carbon film is illustrated in Fig. 1. The p-type silicon substrates, with an electrical resistivity of 7∼13 Ω cm and a thickness of 525 ± 20 μm, were purchased from Resemi Co. Ltd. The silicon substrates were firstly ultrasonically cleaned with a mixture of acetone and ethanol, and then the substrates were immersed into the 5 % HF aqueous solution for 5 mins to remove the oxide layer. The metal layer of Au was deposited by electron beam evaporation at a deposition rate of 0.5 Å/s with thicknesses of 5 nm, 15 nm, and 25 nm, respectively. After depositing the Au, the substrates were cut into squares with 25 mm × 25 mm. The substrates were annealed under a nitrogen atmosphere under 900 °C for 2 h in a vacuum tube furnace and then cooled to room temperature under the nitrogen atmosphere. After the annealing process, the Au layer underwent a transformation into Au nanoparticles. Subsequently, the silicon substrates were etched in oxidizing HF aqueous solutions (HF: 5 mol/L; H2O2: 0.1 mol/L), resulting in the selective etching of the silicon beneath the Au nanoparticles and creating the nanotexture on silicon substrate. The nanotexture depth was regulated with the etching time, which was set at 2 min, 5 min, and 8 min. Then the Au nanoparticles were eliminated with aqua regia. The silicon substrates with nanotexture were placed in the vacuum chamber of the electron cyclotron resonance (ECR) electron sputtering system to deposit the GSEC film. The details about the equipment and the ECR irradiation process were introduced in the former works [17,27]. The GSEC films were obtained by applying a +100 V substrate bias and the deposition rate was 5 nm/min. In this work, the thickness of the GSEC film was set as 100 nm.

A scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) was utilized to observe the morphology of the silicon with Au nanoparticle, the nanotexture present in the silicon, and the nanotexture within the carbon film. In order to demonstrate the correlation between the depth of the nanotexture in the substrate and the etching time, measurements were taken using an Atomic Force Microscope (AFM, INNOVA). The diameter distribution of the nanotexture in silicon substrate conformed to a normal distribution, and statistical analysis was performed using mathematical methods. The surface roughnesses of the carbon films and nanotextured carbon films were measured with AFM. The nanostructure of nanotextured carbon films was examined utilizing a JEM-2100 transmission electron microscope (TEM) operating at a 200 kV electron acceleration voltage. The distribution and dimensions of the graphene sheets incorporated within carbon films were examined with a HORIBA Raman spectrometer equipped with a 532 nm wavelength laser.

A Ball-on-Disk tribometer with a diameter of 3.17 mm Si3N4 counter-grinding ball was utilized to measure the wear life and the friction coefficient of the carbon films. The tests were conducted under room temperature conditions with a relative humidity range of 35 % to 45 %. Here, the sliding velocity was set at 26.4 mm/s with a 1.4 mm frictional radius and a 180 rpm rotating speed. The normal load was set as 1 N. Each sample underwent three measurements to determine the mean value.

The introduction of nanotexture at the interface of the substrate and carbon film noticeably enhanced the adhesion strength, attributed to the mechanical interlocking effect of the nanotexture. To quantitatively characterize the substrate-film adhesion, nano-scratch measurements of the carbon film were conducted using a nanomechanical measurement system (Hysitron TI-950) [37]. During the nano-scratch test, a diamond conical indenter with a tip radius of 5 μm was indented into the carbon film with a linearly increased normal load. Within 200 s, the normal load applied to the tip was linearly increased from 0 to 500 mN, while the tip moved 200 μm along a straight path. The friction force was monitored during the scratch test process, and the morphology of the scratch was observed after the test to determine the critical load at which point the carbon film delaminated from the substrate.

The morphology and nanostructure of transfer films at the surface of the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball were observed with Axio Scope A1 optical microscopy and HORIBA Raman spectrum, respectively. Detailed information on the D and G bands of the Raman spectrum was obtained through Gaussian fitting of the Raman characteristic peaks. According to the intensities of the D (ID) and G bands (IG), as well as the constant value C(λ) associated with the wavelength of the Raman laser, the graphene sheet size Lα could be figured up with the formula 1[38,39]:(1)ID/IG=CλLα2In this case, with a laser wavelength of 532 nm, the corresponding C(λ) value was determined to be 0.55 nm−2.

To further explore the advantage of the nanotexture, the abrasive dust was collected from carbon films with no texture, microtexture, and nanotexture, and their sizes were measured with a nanoparticle size analyzer (Zetasizer Nano ZSE). After the friction test, the wear scar was rinsed with slow-flowing ultrapure water and then collected the water with abrasive dust. The size of the abrasive dust was measured. The transfer films formed during the initial stage of the friction process for the three types of carbon films mentioned above were observed.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Characterization of interface nanotextured carbon films
ce:section.ce:para: The surface morphologies of the Au nanoparticle, produced from the Au layer with thicknesses of 5 nm, 15 nm, and 25 nm, annealed under a nitrogen atmosphere are shown in Fig. 2(a)∼(c). The Au nanoparticle emerged in the shape of a rounded rectangle. As the thickness of the Au film was decreased, the shape of the nanoparticles shifted progressively towards a circular form. The size of the nanoparticle increased with the thickness of the Au layer and the diameter of the nanoparticle varied within a specific range in the same sample. Correspondingly, Fig. 2(d)∼(f) presents images of the nanotexture in the silicon substrate created by metal-assisted chemical etching. Comparing the shape and size of the Au nanoparticles and the nanotexture, it was observed that the metal-assisted chemical etching could replicate the profile of the nanoparticle onto the substrate. Hence, the size of the nanotexture in the silicon substrate could be adjusted by the thickness of the Au layer deposited by electron beam evaporation. After depositing the carbon film, the morphology is illustrated in Fig. 2(g)∼(i). When the Au layer thickness was 5 nm, the carbon film did not exhibit obvious texture. However, as the thickness of the Au layer increased, surface nanotextures gradually began to appear in the carbon film, especially when the Au layer thickness reached 25 nm.

To obtain the diameter distribution of the nanotexture in Fig. 2(d)∼(f), the images were subjected to image binarization. After converting to a binary image, the area of the nanotexture was mathematically analyzed. For simplicity, the diameter of the nanotexture was estimated based on its area, assuming that the nanotexture had a circular shape. The distribution of the nanotexture diameter is shown in Fig. 3. It is evident that the diameter distribution follows a normal pattern. For better analysis of the distribution of the diameter of the nanotexture, the cumulative frequency was added to Fig. 3. Cumulative frequency can intuitively reflect the probability accumulation below each data point in the dataset, which aids in analyzing and understanding the distribution characteristics of the data. According to the cumulative frequency distribution, the diameter distribution of the nanotexture is relatively concentrated. The diameter of the nanotexture ranged from 10 to 60 nm when the Au thickness was 5 nm. As the Au thickness increased to 15 nm, the diameter was from 30 to 150 nm. Finally, when the Au thickness was 25 nm, the nanotexture sizes ranged from 40 nm to 250 nm. Here, the diameter of the nanotextures is represented by the peak of the normal distribution. When the thickness of the Au layer deposited on the silicon was 5 nm, 15 nm, and 25 nm, the diameter of the nanotextured generated by the metal-assisted chemical etching process was represented as 25 nm, 75 nm, and 125 nm, respectively. In addition, the total area was calculated by summing the area of all the etched nanotextures. The surface texture area ratios were 12.1 %, 16.3 %, and 19.5 % for the Au thickness of 5 nm,15 nm, and 25 nm, respectively.

The depth of the nanotexture in the substrate and the surface roughness of carbon films were obtained using the AFM. Fig. 4(a) presents the AFM image of the nanotextured silicon with a nanotexture diameter of 75 nm where the etching time was 5 min. There was a noticeable nanotexture arrangement on the surface of the silicon. The cross-sectional profile of a single nanotexture is depicted in Fig. 4(b). The edge and side walls of the single nanotexture were smooth without obvious rag, and the maximum depth of the texture was 53.2 nm. Similarly, the depths of the nanotexture with etching times of 2 min and 8 min were examined and the nanotexture depth was 21.3 nm and 82.2 nm, respectively. The relationship between nanotexture depth and chemical etching time exhibited an almost linear, with an etching rate of approximately 10 nm/min. In this study, we designated the interface nanotextured carbon film with an interface nanotexture of D nm diameter and H nm depth as ‘nanotextured carbon film D nm-H nm’. Following the deposition of carbon film, the surface roughness of nanotextured carbon film was also examined and summed up in Fig. 4(c). The surface roughness of the carbon film without texture exhibited a value of 10.2 nm, which significantly increased after the addition of the nanotexture. For nanotextured carbon film with the same texture diameter, the roughness increased with the nanotexture depth. Likewise, when the depth of nanotexture was consistent, the roughness also rose with texture diameter. The nanotextured carbon 125 nm-80 nm exhibited the maximum surface roughness, measuring 30.9 nm.

Fig. 2 (g)∼(i) has given the surface morphology of the nanotextured carbon film. To better reveal the interface between the carbon film and nanotextured silicon substrate, the cross-sectional image of the nanotextured carbon film is illustrated in Fig. 5 (a). The SEM image shows that there were obvious nanotextures at the interface between the carbon film and the nanotextured silicon substrate. The introduction of nanotexture into the substrate enlarged the interface area between the substrate and the carbon film. This enhancement led to an increased number of chemical bonds between the carbon film and the substrate. The nanostructure of nanotextured carbon film was measured by TEM with an accelerating voltage of 200 kV. The carbon film nanostructure is shown in Fig. 5 (b), there were obviously delineated graphene nanosheets encircled by a dotted line embedded in the matrix of the amorphous carbon. It indicated that the graphene nanocrystallite still existed in the matrix of amorphous carbon after the addition of the nanotexture. To further examine the impact of the nanotexture on the carbon film, the Raman spectra tests were conducted with both the carbon film with and without nanotexture, and the results are exhibited in Fig. 5(c). After Gaussian fitting of the Raman characteristic peaks, the length of the graphene sheet was calculated using formulation 1. The size of the nanosheets in the initial and the nanotextured carbon films was almost the same. Besides, the Raman spectra obtained from different positions in the nanotextured carbon film were identical. The above results indicated that the nanotexture in the substrate had little effect on the GSEC film nanostructure and the distribution of graphene nanosheets within the carbon film.

For carbon films with and without interface nanotexture, their tribological performance was assessed by the Ball-on-Disk tribometer. The friction curve of GSEC film without nanotexture is illustrated in Fig. 6(a). It could be found that the friction coefficient was 0.18 initially, then increased abruptly to 0.32 after 18 cycles. The value of 0.32 was the friction coefficient between the silicon and the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball. After the friction test, the observation of the wear scar showed that the carbon film wore out during the friction process. In conclusion, the wear life of carbon film without nanotexture was 18 cycles. The friction curves of nanotextured carbon films with different nanotexture depths are displayed in Fig. 6(b). For the nanotextured carbon films with a 75 nm nanotexture diameter, the friction coefficients increased from 0.108 to 0.112 and finally reached 0.132 with increasing texture depth. However, the wear life exhibited an initial increase followed by a subsequent decrease as the depth of the nanotexture increased from 20 nm to 50 nm. The nanotextured carbon film 75 nm-50 nm exhibited the maximum wear life with a value of 67,000 cycles. As illustrated in Fig. 6(c), for the nanotextured carbon films with a texture depth of 50 nm, the friction coefficient increased from 0.109 to 0.13 with the nanotexture diameter from 25 nm to 125 nm. The wear life followed a similar trend with an increase in the nanotexture diameter, and the nanotextured carbon film 25 nm-50 nm exhibited a wear life of 22,700 cycles. Especially, when the texture diameter extended to 125 nm, the carbon film could run smoothly for 90,000 cycles without failure. Comparing the friction curves of carbon films with and without nanotexture, it is evident that the wear life showed an improvement of three orders of magnitude, and the friction coefficient significantly decreased after the addition of interface nanotexture in the GSEC film.

Furthermore, to explore the impact of interface nanotexture parameters on the tribological properties, friction tests were carried out on the nanotextured carbon film with diameters of 25 nm, 50 nm, and 75 nm, and nanotexture depths of 20 nm, 50 nm, and 80 nm. Fig. 7(a)∼(b) provides detailed information about the wear life and friction coefficient of the nanotextured carbon film, respectively. Fig. 7(a) illustrates that the wear life of nanotextured carbon film displayed a tendency to rise initially and then reduce with the nanotexture depth when the diameter of the nanotexture was the same. For nanotextured carbon film with the same nanotexture depth, the wear life increased with the rise in nanotexture diameter. The wear life of nanotextured carbon film significantly surpassed that of the film without texture, and the minimum and maximum wear life appeared in the nanotextured carbon film 25 nm-80 nm and 125 nm-50 nm respectively. The minimum wear life was 3,700 cycles, and the maximum was more than 90,000 cycles. The friction coefficient of nanotextured carbon film showed a significant reduction compared to that of the carbon film without nanotexture, with a value of 0.18. For the nanotextured carbon film with the same nanotexture diameter, the friction coefficient increased as the texture depth. Similarly, the friction coefficient was also raised gradually with the nanotexture diameter when the nanotexture was the same. The minimum and maximum friction coefficients were 0.104 and 0.132, respectively. Above all, it could be noticed that the anti-wear properties of carbon films showed a distinct improvement, moreover, the friction coefficient displayed a distinct decrease following the incorporation of interface nanotexture.

For the nanotextured carbon film 125 nm-50 nm, the wear life was exceeding 90.000 cycles. To better value the wear properties, the cross-section profile of the wear track was measured using 3D profilometry (Dektak XT), and the wear rate was calculated with formula 2:(2)δ=VLWwhere, δ-wear rate, i.e., the wear volume per unit length slid under unit load/mm3·N−1·m−1; V − Wear volume of the carbon film after 90,000 cycles of sliding / mm3; L − Sliding distance of Si3N4 ball for 90,000 cycles; W − Normal load / N.

The cross-sectional profile and the optical image of the wear track after 90,000 cycles of sliding are shown in Fig. 8. The width of the wear track measured 112.2 μm, and its maximum depth was 69.4 nm. Based on the cross-sectional area of the wear track and formula 2, the wear rate of the nanotextured carbon film 125 nm-50 nm was calculated to be 6.54 ± 0.70 × 10−8 mm3/Nm, indicating a super low wear rate. The wear rate was much lower than that reported in other literature, such as the wear rate was about 3 × 10−7 mm3/Nm under dry friction conditions [40], the wear rate was about 8.02 × 10−7 mm3/Nm [41], and the wear rate was about 3 × 10−5 mm3/Nm [42].

According to the above analysis, the friction coefficient of the nanotextured carbon film showed an increase with both the nanotexture diameter and the nanotexture depth. The variation tendency of the friction coefficient aligned with the change in the nanotextured carbon film surface roughness, as illustrated in Fig. 4(d). For the GSEC film, the transfer film on the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball would also have a noticeable effect on the friction coefficient, in addition to the surface roughness. To clarify the effect of the transfer film on the carbon film friction coefficient, the morphology and nanostructure of transfer films on the surface of the Si3N4 ball were measured after running 5,000 cycles. The transfer films of the nanotextured carbon films with different nanotexture diameters under a 50 nm texture depth were tested, as illustrated in Fig. 9(a)∼(d). The transfer film optical images of the nanotextured carbon with different diameters are illustrated in Fig. 9(a)∼(c). There was a smooth and continuous transfer film on the Si3N4 ball, which could reduce the friction coefficient and make sure the friction process stably runs. Fig. 9(d) presents the corresponding Raman spectrum of the transfer film, and the tested spot was marked in the image of the transfer film. There were distinct D and G bands in the Raman spectra, which indicated that there is a nanocrystal graphene within the transfer film. Furthermore, the length of graphene nanosheets was deduced using Eq. (1). The length of the graphene nanosheets decreased from 1.29 nm to 1.25 nm with the nanotexture diameter extended from 25 nm to 75 nm. Finally, when the nanotexture diameter was 125 nm, the length of the graphene nanosheets was 1.22 nm. The nanocrystallization of transfer films was the strongest for the nanotextured carbon film with a 25 nm texture diameter. According to the previous study [43], the length of the graphene nanosheets in the transfer film was affected the friction coefficient. This could potentially explain the increasing trend in the friction coefficient with the diameter of the nanotexture.

To analyze the effect of the texture diameter on the contact area. The radius (a0) of the contact area was calculated by the Hertzian contact formula of spherical contact.(3)a0=3WR04E∗13(4)E∗=11-μ12E1+1-μ22E2where a0 is the radius of the contact area and R0 is the radius of the Si3N4 ball (R0 = 3.175 mm). μ1 and μ2 are Poisson's ratios of carbon film and Si3N4 ball, respectively. The value of μ1 is 0.3 and μ2 is 0.22. E1 and E2 are the elastic moduli of carbon film and Si3N4 ball respectively. The value of E1 is 142.3 GPa and E2 is 336.9 GPa. According to Eq. (3), the radius (a0) of the contact area was 44.4 μm. In this work, the diameter of the nanotexture was much lower than the contact area between the carbon film and the Si3N4 ball, resulting in the effect of the nanotexture being little of the contact area. Besides, according to the transfer film images in Fig. 9, the contact area of the nanotextured carbon film with different texture diameters was almost the same, and the radius of the contact area was about 47.1 μm, which was close to the calculated result of the carbon without texture. Therefore, the effects of the paraments nanotexture on the contact area were little.

To clarify the frictional behavior of the carbon film with nanotexture, surface morphologies of the transfer film on the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball were observed after running different cycles. Fig. 10 shows the evolution of the shape of the transfer film for the nanotextured carbon film 75 nm-50 nm after running 5,000 cycles, 15,000 cycles, and 50,000 cycles. Before testing, the Si3N4 ball was wiped with acetone and dried with dry air. According to the analysis above, there was a smooth and continuous transfer film on the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball and the transfer film contained the graphene nanosheets after running 5,000 cycles. The transfer film still kept a continuous shape when the friction process was conducted at 15,000 cycles. However, when the friction cycles reached 50,000 cycles, the integrity of the transfer film was broken, and there was a little breakage in the transfer film.

For the carbon film with interface nanotexture, the adhesion strength between the silicon substrate and carbon film would be enhanced extensively, resulting in an improved anti-wear performance of carbon films. To clarify the influence of the nanotexture on the adhesion strength between the silicon substrate and carbon film, the nano-scratch tests were conducted on the carbon films with and without the nanotexture. According to the friction force variation during the scratch testing process and the optical image of the scratch, the critical load under which the carbon film peels off the silicon substrate was confirmed. Fig. 11(a) and Fig. 11(b) give the scratch test results of the nanotextured carbon film 75 nm-50 nm. The friction force rose gradually with the normal load until it reached 282.6 mN, at which point a sudden fluctuation occurred in the friction force. Correspondingly, from the optical image of the scratch, the carbon film peels off from the substrate at 112 μm in the scratch. Thus, the critical load of the nanotextured carbon film 75 nm-50 nm was determined to be 282.6 mN. In the same manner, the critical loads of the carbon films with different nanotexture parameters were obtained. Fig. 11(c) illustrates the variation in critical load and wear life with different nanotexture diameters at a depth of 50 nm. After the addition of the nanotexture, both the wear resistance of the carbon film and the film-substrate adhesion strength showed improvements over those without nanotextures. With the nanotexture depth remaining constant, the wear life and adhesion strength of the nanotextured carbon film increased simultaneously as the nanotexture diameter increased. This tendency was also consistent with a change in surface texture area ratio in the silicon substrate with the nanotexture diameter. Hence, for the nanotextured carbon film with the same nanotexture depth, the strength of film-substrate adhesion mainly determines the anti-wear performance of nanotextured carbon films. As shown in Fig. 11(d), for nanotextured carbon film with the same diameter, the film-substrate adhesion also increased with nanotexture depth. However, the variation of the wear life with nanotexture depth initially rose and then dropped. This could be attributed to the depth of surface nanotextures and surface roughness increasing with the depth of the nanotexture, which caused more severe wear in the initial stage of the friction process. Consequently, for nanotextured carbon films with the same diameter, the wear life demonstrated an initial increase followed by a subsequent decrease as the nanotexture depth increased under the combined action of these two factors.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Role of nanotexture in the wear performance
ce:section.ce:para: To better understand the advantage of the nanotexture, the frictional behavior of carbon films with no texture, microtexture, and nanotexture was compared. Fig. 12(a)∼(c) gives the transfer films on the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball observed after running 20 cycles. For the carbon film without texture, there was lots of abrasive dust accumulated on the Si3N4 ball instead of the stable transfer film due to the failure of the carbon film. There is a very thin transfer film on the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball for the carbon film with microtexture. However, for the carbon film with nanotexture, a stable and thick transfer film was generated on the Si3N4 ball after running only 20 cycles. In the case of carbon film without texture, abrasive dust was collected after the film broke. For the carbon film with microtexture and nanotexture, the abrasive dust was collected after running 300 cycles. The particle size distribution of abrasive dust is illustrated in Fig. 12(d). The size of the abrasive dust follows a normal distribution. The average size of the abrasive dust was calculated with the size and the probability by Eq. (5):(5)E(s)=∑sipiwhere si was the size of the abrasive dust, pi was the probability when the size of the abrasive dust was si. E(s) was the average size of the abrasive dust.

The average size of the abrasive dust was 206 nm for carbon film without texture. After adding the microtexture, the size of the abrasive slightly increased, reaching 242 nm. However, for the nanotextured carbon film, the abrasive size showed a significant decrease, with a value of 81 nm.

According to the above result, the frictional process of the GSEC film with and without texture was clarified. As displayed in Fig. 13(a), for carbon film without nanotexture, the carbon film broke under the preliminary friction process stage due to poor film-substrate adhesion strength. A large amount of abrasive in the friction interface results in a high friction coefficient. For carbon film with interface texture, the enhanced adhesion strength ensured smooth running during the early stage of the friction process. As displayed in Fig. 13(b), for the carbon film with microtexture, due to the contact stress on the edge of the texture, the size of the abrasive dust increased slightly. The surface microtexture could store the abrasive resulting in a reduction of the friction coefficient. However, as a portion of the abrasive debris is retained within the texture, this can lead to a reduction in the transfer of debris to the surface of the grinding ball, thereby prolonging the process of the formation of the transfer film. Conversely, as depicted in Fig. 12(c), for the carbon film with nanotexture, the nanotexture could reduce the size of the abrasive dust in the friction interface. The ability of the nanotexture to store abrasive dust was relatively weak, which facilitated the generation of the stable transfer film containing graphene nanosheets quickly. The smaller abrasive dust and stable transfer film resulted in a stable friction process for the carbon film.

In this work, the interface nanotextured graphene sheet-embedded carbon (GSEC) films were fabricated with the Au-assisted chemical etching process and the low-energy electron irradiation process. The diameter and depth of the nanotexture on the silicon substrate were adjusted by the thickness of the Au layer and the etching time of the Au-assisted chemical etching process, respectively. The nanotexture had little effect on the nanostructure of the GSEC film and the distribution of the graphene nanosheets compared to the carbon film without nanotexture. The introduction of nanotexture into the substrate enlarged the interface area between the substrate and the carbon film. This enhancement led to an increased number of chemical bonds between the carbon film and the substrate. Furthermore, the interlocking between the substrate and the carbon film enhances adhesion strength, effectively preventing the peeling of the carbon film and improving its wear resistance. Besides, the surface nanotexture could reduce the size of the abrasive dust, and the limited ability to store abrasive dust by nanotexture could facilitate the generation of the stable transfer film containing graphene nanosheets quickly, which ensures the friction process smoothly runs. Throughout the friction process, a stable transfer film comprising graphene nanosheets was observed on the surface of the Si3N4 counter-grinding ball. This transfer film effectively reduced the friction coefficient by the weak Van der Waals force between the layers of graphene. The wear life and friction coefficient of nanotextured carbon films were greatly affected by the parameters of the nanotexture. The friction coefficient of the nanotextured carbon film was much lower than the carbon film without texture and the lowest value was 0.104. The nanotextured GSEC film exhibited a maximum wear life exceeding 90,000 cycles and the wear rate was 6.54 ± 0.70 × 10−8 mm3/Nm, indicating a super-low wear rate. These explorations could facilitate the application of functional thin films.
